abstract: ABSTRACT This paper proposes an intelligent industrial setpoint tracking control approach using an output recurrent elliptic fuzzy broad learning system (Elliptic ORFBLS). This approach integrates the strengths of intelligent control, which effectively manages complex nonlinear systems with an adaptive identification mechanism that efficiently handles uncertain parameters in unknown systems. The adaptive mechanism notably enhances transient state responses, leading to faster rise times and reduced overshoot, while ensuring stable and precise setpoint tracking in the steady state. Three theorems are presented to guarantee system convergence, stability, and applicability. Additionally, a comprehensive study on time complexity and memory consumption is included to assist practitioners in controller selection. Through comparative simulations and experimental validations, this control strategy is shown to offer a robust and effective solution for challenging nonlinear systems.
title: Intelligent Industrial Setpoint Tracking Control Using Output Recurrent Elliptic Fuzzy Broad Learning System

abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are designed to anchor large language models in verified evidence. In controlled settings, retrieval improves factual accuracy and reduces hallucination risk. In production environments, however, an under-examined failure mode is emerging. Stacked safety layers surrounding the generation stage can subtly distort how retrieved evidence is expressed, resulting in answers that remain compliant but become diluted, hedged, or operationally weakened. This paper defines this phenomenon as the Guardrail Shadow Effect (GSE). The proposed framework introduces the Shadow Impact Score (SIS) to quantify when high-quality retrieved context fails to translate into proportionate answer strength. Rather than auditing safety filters or retrieval quality in isolation, the method models cross-layer interaction between retrieval confidence, policy pressure, and generation behaviour. The architecture is model-agnostic and suitable for enterprise knowledge copilots, regulated-domain assistants, and internal RAG deployments. Evaluation across controlled simulations shows that guardrail pressure can materially reduce evidence utilization even when retrieval precision remains stable. The findings expose a structural blind spot in current RAG observability: grounding can succeed while usefulness quietly degrades. Detecting and managing guardrail shadow dynamics will be essential for organizations that want RAG systems to remain both safe and decisively useful.
title: Guardrail Shadow Effects in Retrieval-Augmented Systems (Safety Layers Distorting RAG Outputs)

abstract: Generative large-language models (LLMs) are evolving from passive tools into adaptive cognitive partners. This paper proposes the Hybrid Agency Framework (HAF), a conceptual model that treats the human-LLM dyad as a single, integrated cybernetic system. Drawing from the traditions of joint cognitive systems and control theory, HAF moves beyond the prevalent "blind prompting" paradigm, where users operate with limited insight into the model's state and bear full liability for its outputs. We formalize the collaborative process as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), providing a principled, control-theoretic foundation for managing interaction. The framework's central contribution is a model of bidirectional alignment, where both the human's expressed preferences and the LLM's policy co-adapt in real-time within a shared cognitive workspace. This contrasts sharply with current one-way alignment methods (e.g., RLHF) that treat user preferences as static targets for model training. Furthermore, HAF integrates a multi-stakeholder governance matrix explicitly mapped to emerging regulatory standards (EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001) to distribute accountability. This paper presents the complete conceptual design, including its theoretical underpinnings, a formal POMDP specification, a multifactor skill-retention protocol to mitigate user de-skilling, and a detailed plan for future empirical validation. By framing human-LLM interaction as a controllable cybernetic system, HAF offers a rigorous roadmap toward safer, more transparent, and genuinely collaborative hybrid intelligence.
title: A Hybrid Agency Framework: Modeling Human-LLM Interaction as a Cybernetic System

abstract: This study explores the integration of a pre-trained Large Language Model (LLM) with an organisation's Knowledge Management System (KMS) via a chat interface, focusing on the practicalities of establishing and maintaining AI infrastructure for data storage and access, and the considerations to ensure responsible governance. The study adopts the concept of ‘AI as a constituted system’ to emphasise that the social, technical, and institutional factors that contribute to AI’s governance and accountability. Through an ethnographic approach, the paper details the iterative processes of negotiation, decision-making, and reflection among stakeholders as they develop, implement, and manage the AI system. The study reveals that LLMs can be effectively governed and held accountable to the interests of stakeholders within specific contexts, when facilitated by clear institutional boundaries that foster innovation, while navigating risks related to data privacy and AI misbehaviours. This is attributed to distinct policy creation processes guiding the AI's operation, clear lines of responsibility, and localised feedback loops that ensured clear accountability for actions taken. This research offers a foundational perspective to better understand accountability and governance of algorithms within organisational contexts. It also suggests a future where AI is not universally scaled but consists of localised, customised LLMs that are tailored to stakeholder interests.
title: AI as a Constituted System: Accountability Lessons from an LLM Experiment

abstract: Abstract Industrial surface defect inspection and automatic sorting control constitute critical feedback links in intelligent manufacturing cybernetic systems. Conventional detection methods suffer from bulky model parameters, low inference speed, and weak anti-interference capability under uneven illumination, tiny defect targets and surface occlusion, failing to satisfy the millisecond-level closed-loop feedback constraints of industrial production control. Targeting the disconnection between machine learning visual detection and industrial automatic control in existing YOLO-based research, this paper proposes a lightweight adaptive YOLOv11 detector and constructs a complete machine-learning-perception-driven closed-loop sorting cybernetic control system. First, a Lightweight Coordinate Adaptive Attention (LCAA) module is embedded into the YOLOv11 C2f backbone to boost feature extraction for tiny blurred defects while compressing redundant parameters. Second, an adaptive multi-scale feature fusion mechanism is designed for the neck network to dynamically adjust fusion weights according to target scale variation, mitigating multi-scale defect missing detection. Finally, the optimized lightweight model is deployed on edge embedded hardware, and real-time detection outputs act as state feedback signals for the sorting controller to establish a full perception-decision-execution negative feedback control loop. Experiments on the public NEU steel defect dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 97.2% mAP@0.5, with parameters reduced by 28.6% and inference speed increased by 32.1% compared with vanilla YOLOv11. Physical edge sorting platform tests verify the closed-loop system maintains an overall end-to-end delay below 50 ms, sorting success rate of 98.5% and steady-state error less than 2%. This work delivers an integrated machine learning perception-cybernetic control solution for industrial intelligent manufacturing, matching the interdisciplinary positioning of machine learning and cybernetics.
title: Lightweight Adaptive YOLOv11 for Industrial Defect Perception and Closed-Loop Sorting Cybernetic Control System

abstract: Abstract Road safety is a major global concern nowadays. Within the road infrastructure, bridge sectors are the most dangerous in terms of the incidence and severity of accidents. Engineering practice is to reduce their gravity by installing safety barriers with a very high level of protection, type H4b. There are however situations in which these protection systems actually and up reducing the level of safety for road users by limiting visibility. This paper studies the possibility of adopting an innovative safety barrier solution based on modern, more efficient materials such as prestressed high-strength steel reinforcement. Scaled model of 1:20 tests and numerical simulations are presented for a guardrail system made up of high strength cables and plastic hinge supports.

abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to multi-disease diagnosis using a lightweight neural network architecture combined with large language model (LLM) powered explanations. We demonstrate how modern AI assistants can enable rapid development of functional healthcare AI systems with minimal code implementation. Our system achieves 72% accuracy on synthetic multi-disease classification tasks (Diabetes, Parkinson's Disease, and Healthy classifications) while providing human-readable explanations for each diagnosis through an integrated LLM reasoning module. The complete system, implemented in under 500 lines of code, demonstrates end-to-end functionality from data generation to model deployment, showcasing the potential for democratizing AI healthcare development. Key contributions include: (1) a streamlined architecture combining neural networks with LLM explanations, (2) automatic symbolic rule extraction for high-confidence predictions, (3) a deployable model export system, and (4) transparent documentation of AI-assisted development methodologies.

abstract: ABSTRACT Distributed bioenergy renewable power networks face an unresolved equity challenge: AI‐governed dispatch optimisers maximise aggregate throughput while systematically under‐serving peripheral nodes. This paper presents ethical guardrail bandit pruning, a fairness‐constrained reinforcement learning system enforcing equity and energy sustainability via a two‐timescale primal‐dual guardrail, coupling a bandit‐gradient importance estimator, an ethical guardrail buffer, cost‐weighted pruning and guardrail‐filtered federated averaging over a constrained Markov decision process. Three theorems establish regret optimality, convergence and a federated exclusion bound. The integrated system was empirically verified across 16 seeds at 60 communication rounds, with no catastrophic instability (maximum Gini below 0.28) and steady‐state Gini 0.188 versus an unconstrained baseline of 0.805, confirmed by ablation and sensitivity analysis. Convergence was checked against logged gradient norms and found shallower than theory predicts. A 5000‐round extended‐horizon run (50,000 local steps) remained within the safety threshold in of rounds; multi‐seed extended‐horizon verification is future work. Results operationalise SDG 7, 10, 12 and 13 as verifiable engineering guardrails.
title: Ethical Guardrail Bandit Pruning (EGBP): A Fairness‐Constrained Reinforcement Learning System for Equitable Governance of Distributed Bioenergy Grids

abstract: Industrial AI methods for detection, recognition, and prediction share an entry condition that is rarely stated: the problem must first be formalized into defined objects, variables, and labels. For high-value, cross-domain, system-level non-standard problems, formalization is itself the most expensive step, with costs arising at the physical, cognitive, and organizational levels. The consequence is a selection effect. Problems that can be formalized get solved and leave the pool; the problems that accumulate on the shop floor are systematically those hardest to formalize. Large language models do not require prior formalization. What they change is the cost structure of problem definition, not the physical difficulty of the problem. The study then proposes an L1–L4 grading with a six-feature complexity criterion and a five-stage human–LLM collaborative framework. Validation draws on eight real industrial cases spanning steel rolling, water treatment, continuous-casting electrics, materials development, industrial software, and industrial networks. In the two in-depth cases the complexity score fell from 15 to 7 and 8, with the drop concentrated in the structural items that capture definition difficulty; of three independent double ratings, two agreed at band level and the third fell one band adjacent. A contrasting pair of third-party collaborations marks where the mechanism stops: executed under the framework, a months-long intermittent fault was localized within half a day; used as naive question-answering, the collaboration did not converge, because a key temporal cue never entered the problem representation. On this evidence the binding constraint is representation completeness rather than model capability.
title: The Formalization Threshold and Selection Effect: A Complexity Grading Criterion and Human–LLM Framework from Eight Industrial Cases

abstract: Agentic AI systems introduce novel safety challenges that upstream alignment layers cannot fully address. Prompt injection, emotional manipulation, and infrastructure-disabling actions can bypass model-level safeguards, leading to unauthorized tool executions with real-world consequences. We present Guardian Angel, a deployable plugin for open agent frameworks (e.g., OpenClaw/ClawHub) that enforces moral oversight at the last mile-immediately before tool calls-via a privileged before_tool_call hook. Grounded in Thomistic virtue ethics and centered on caritas (the willing of the principal's genuine good), the system maintains a continuous virtuous disposition while applying triggered three-gate evaluation: provenance classification, intrinsic-evil hard stops, and virtue-based scoring using a Clarity × Stakes matrix. Questionable actions escalate to human approval via cryptographically bound, time-limited nonces. The design exploits a key structural property of agentic systems-the sparsity of tool calls relative to internal reasoning-to integrate fast System 1 filtering with deliberate System 2 moral reasoning, thereby decentralizing safety to end-users without prohibitive latency. We discuss the philosophical prerequisites for such systems, detail the architecture and implementation, present qualitative evaluation results from red-team testing, and outline directions for formal benchmarking. Guardian Angel is MIT-0 licensed and available at https://clawhub.ai/leo3linbeck/guardian-angel.
title: Guardian Angel: A Last-Mile Virtue-Ethics Guardrail for Decentralized Agentic AI Safety

abstract: Abstract Industrial robot is a and multi‐output complex system with strong coupling and high nonlinearity. The motion control accuracy of the system is affected by many factors. To solve the difficulty in establishing the input and output characteristics of robot dynamics modeling, the robot motion model is established through the Lagrangian energy function. At the same time, the nonlinear relationship between angular velocity, angular acceleration, and robot torque is accurately expressed through improved cascaded neural network. In addition, the optimal time planning of the robot's trajectory in joint space is studied using multinomial interpolation method and the particle swarm optimization (PSO). In the simulation experiment, the effect of the proposed dynamic model fitting was outstanding. Under the mixed multinomial difference calculation planning, the angular position trajectories of the three joints changed very smoothly. In the data set application test, the average error of the PSO algorithm was 0.4061 mm and the average task time was 9.101 s, which were lower than other planning algorithms. Experiments showed that the Lagrangian dynamic model analysis based on genetic algorithm cascaded neural network and PSO trajectory scheduling method under mixed multinomial difference had better trajectory planning performance in handling tasks.
title: Design of nonlinear control system for motion trajectory of industrial handling robot
venue: Advanced Control for Applications

abstract: With the development of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) technology, multimachine collaborative operations have become the core model for increasing mission effectiveness. However, large-scale UAV clusters face challenges such as dynamic security threats, heterogeneous data fusion difficulties, and resource-constrained decision-making delays. Traditional single-machine intelligent architectures have limitations when addressing new threats, such as insufficient real-time response capabilities. To address these issues, this paper presnts an LLM-layered collaborative security architecture (LLM-LCSA) for multimachine collaborative security. This architecture optimizes the spatiotemporal fusion efficiency of multisource asynchronous data through cloud–edge–end collaborative deployment, combining an end lightweight LLM, an edge medium LLM, and a cloud-based foundation LLM. Additionally, a Mixture of Experts (MoEs) intelligent algorithm that dynamically activates the most relevant expert models by leveraging a threat–expert association matrix is introduced, thereby increasing the accuracy of complex threat identification and dynamic adaptability. Moreover, a resource-aware multi-objective optimization model is constructed to generate optimal decisions under resource constraints. Simulation results indicate that compared with traditional methods, LLM-LCSA achieves an average 7.92% improvement in the threat detection accuracy, reduces the system’s total response time by 44.52%, and enables resource scheduling during off-peak periods. This architecture provides an efficient, intelligent, and scalable solution for secure collaboration among UAV swarms. Future research should further explore its application potential in 6G network integration and large-scale swarm environments.
title: LLM-LCSA: LLM for Collaborative Control and Decision Optimization in UAV Cluster Security
venue: Drones

abstract: This work is devoted to the design of a decision-support architecture for artificial intelligence agents used in higher-education. The paper proposes a priority-ordered decision model that ranks three evaluation signals – divergence between self-assessment and teacher assessment, performance trend, and peer comparison – before any call to a language model, so that the same input data always yields the same intervention priority. The model is based on a deterministic progress-weighting service defined by equations (1) – (9), with a course-configurable divergence threshold (τ = 0.15 in the reference configuration) and four weight coefficients that sum to 1. The paper develops a reference implementation with a typed evidence schema, a FastAPI backend, and a tool-augmented LLM agent restricted to four read-only tools. A worked example shows that a flagged divergence (d = 0.25 > τ) overrides an improving trend (L: 0.58 → 0.64 → 0.67), correctly prioritizing a calibration alert over a routine update. The results can be used to design auditable, LLM-based recommendation systems for education and other domains where several evidence signals must be reconciled before a generative model is invoked.
title: A Priority-ordered Decision Model for Educational LLM Agents
venue: Electronics and Control Systems

abstract: This chapter introduces a modular architectural framework for securing the lifecycle of autonomous intelligent systems. As AI transitions from traditional data processing to advanced Knowledge Engineering, the necessity for robust safety mechanisms becomes critical. This article describes how to integrate multi-vector guardrails—specifically focusing on backend validation, real-time adversarial purification, and deterministic logic—into the control flow of autonomous agents. The speedy development of agentic AI in recent years has made it a popular direction for research in smart applications, but it also introduces risks such as data poisoning and model hallucinations. This study presents an efficient approach to mitigating these risks by implementing a layered security architecture. The research evaluates the effectiveness of these safety protocols without compromising computational performance, providing a blueprint for inherently secure intelligent systems.

abstract: Objetivo: Diseñar e implementar un asistente conversacional multimodal embebido en hardware de borde para entornos industriales, resolviendo la ausencia de interfaces locales especializadas en la atención comercial y técnica. Metodología: Mediante investigación aplicada, se desarrolló una arquitectura modular integrada en una tarjeta NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier. El sistema sincroniza tres formas de interacción mediante procesamiento multihilo: visión artificial con MediaPipe para activación gestual; procesamiento bidireccional de voz con Whisper para transcripción (STT) y motores híbridos para síntesis (TTS); e inferencia local mediante Ollama. Para optimizar el rendimiento y asegurar baja latencia sin dependencia de la nube, se aplicó procesamiento selectivo por lotes, fragmentación de texto (chunking) en el TTS y optimización en GPU CUDA. La validación experimental evaluó la consistencia semántica y el consumo de hardware desplegando el modelo ligero Qwen2.5 (500 millones de parámetros) alimentado con una base de conocimiento corporativa. Resultados: Las pruebas demostraron estabilidad operativa e interacciones libres de alucinaciones. El sistema registró una latencia promedio de 17.24 ms por token, rendimiento de 58.53 tokens por segundo, y un consumo eficiente de recursos del 22.69% en memoria y 10.77% en CPU. Discusiones: La fluidez y longitud de las respuestas continuas se encuentran supeditadas a la tasa de compresión de tokens del modelo de lenguaje y a la latencia inherente del motor de traducción de voz. Conclusiones: El desarrollo valida la viabilidad de ejecutar modelos de lenguaje pequeños en la periferia industrial. Su diseño modular y la flexibilidad para reconfigurar roles mediante archivos de texto garantizan su escalabilidad en la Industria 5.0.

abstract: The development of industrial robotics technology has led to a large number of applications in assembly tasks in production practice, but due to factors such as the complexity of the assembly process, the robot's own positioning accuracy and the limitations of vision technology, there are still great challenges in the control of high-precision assembly of robots. In this paper, a high-precision assembly industrial robot automatic control and servo control system combined with flexible assembly technology is proposed. In this system, an actuation system and a mechanics perception system are designed. The actuation system is based on 6PUS-UPU parallel robots, and the motion control of the assembly robot is realized by kinematic inverse solution. The mechanics sensing system is constructed based on a six-dimensional force sensor as a way to obtain the force/torque data during the assembly process of the industrial robot. Then the robot motion model is linearized using the variational method, and then an ideal impedance model is set for the adjustable parametric impedance control system to realize the supple control of the industrial robot with reference to the adaptive control method. It is found that the optimized automatic control and servo control system of the high-precision assembly industrial robot in this paper has higher assembly efficiency and strong fault-tolerant assembly effect. Therefore, the optimization of the automatic control and servo control system of high-precision assembly industrial robots can lay a solid foundation for improving the industrial production level.
title: Optimization research on automatic control and servo control system of high-precision assembly industrial robot based on variational method

abstract: Industrial data-center systems contain complex component dependencies and long fault-propagation chains, making accurate root-cause localization difficult. Large language models (LLMs) provide a promising solution because of their strong ability to understand, organize, and reason over heterogeneous operational evidence. However, existing LLM-based methods mainly rely on statistical co-occurrence in pretraining corpora and may mistake correlation for causation in complex systems. In this paper, we propose CALM, a causally constrained LLM framework for fault diagnosis. The main idea is to learn the causal structure among fault units induced by system dependencies and use it to constrain the LLM reasoning process. Specifically, we train a graph neural network with independently learnable edge gates, impose sparsity directly on these gates, and validate the retained edges using post-training nonlinear Granger predictive gains. The resulting causal relationships constrain the LLM to trace root causes reliably. Experiments on a dataset collected from a power metering data center show that the proposed method achieves a root-cause localization accuracy of 82.6%, outperforming the best-performing baseline by 9.2 percentage points. The method also outputs explicit fault-propagation paths, indicating that causal-structure constraints can improve both the accuracy and interpretability of fault diagnosis.
title: Causal Graph Constrained LLM for Fault Diagnosis in Industrial Data Centers

abstract: The limited accessibility, high cost, and low scalability of industrial control platforms constrain hands-on learning in automation education. This study presents a real-time control system architecture that bridges instructional requirements with industrial control principles through deterministic execution and structured logic representation. The system integrates ladder-based programming with cyclic scan execution and direct I/O mapping to ensure consistent real-time operation. A design and development methodology based on the adopted-ADDIE framework was employed to guide system realization and validation. The system was evaluated through expert-based assessment using a four-point Likert scale, followed by feasibility, content validity, and reliability analyses. Results indicate high technical feasibility, with technical quality reaching 83.04% and display quality 84.38% (very feasible), while instructional aspects range from 75.00% to 79.55% (feasible). Content validity achieved Aiken’s V values of 0.852 (very high) and 0.716 (high), with reliable expert agreement (Sig. > 0.05). These findings validate the proposed architecture as a scalable and reliable control system platform for automation learning.
title: Bridging Control System Education and Industrial Practice through a Real-Time Control System Architecture

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are predominantly controlled through parameter-level optimization, with fine-tuning often treated as the primary mechanism for behavioral alignment and specialization. While effective in many contexts, fine-tuning alone operates over globally distributed training data, leaving inference vulnerable to coherence loss when reasoning spans distant or weakly related knowledge regions-an effect frequently associated with hallucination phenomena. This paper argues that fine-tuning should not be regarded as the sole legitimate axis of behavioral control in LLM-based systems. We introduce overtuning, a non-parametric control paradigm that governs model behavior externally through an orchestration layer, without modifying model weights. Central to this approach is the concept of a metaprompt: a software-mediated control artifact responsible for dynamically assembling, constraining, and injecting context-aware prompts into one or multiple LLMs based on persistent memory, pre-registered policies, and execution-time conditions. We present a minimal executable framework in which overtuning reduces effective inferential distance by anchoring generation to dynamically maintained contextual and mnemonic pillars, thereby mitigating hallucination risk through constraint rather than additional learning. Beyond contextual grounding, the framework supports ethical enforcement, role scoping, behavioral routing, and auditability via specialized constraint modules operating at the orchestration level. At the same time, we explicitly address a critical risk of overtuning: excessive internal coherence may lead to epistemic enclosure, where systems become circularly self-consistent and insufficiently exposed to external reference signals-a phenomenon analogous to Plato's Cave. We argue that this risk does not invalidate overtuning, but instead defines concrete governance requirements, including de-circularization mechanisms, external refresh policies, and formal system-level invariants. By formalizing overtuning as a distinct control axis and articulating its architectural benefits and limits, this work contributes a governance-oriented alternative to parameter-centric alignment, with direct implications for explainability, auditability, and the design of controllable AI systems.
title: Overtuning by Metaprompt: A Non-Parametric Control Axis for LLM Behavior

abstract: Textile industries are responsible for one of the major environmental pollution because they release undesirable dye effluents. Therefore, environmental legislation commonly obligates textile factories to treat these effluents before discharge into the water bodies. The main aim of this paper is to control the parameters causing pollution and to reduce the effect of these parameters and controlling them without affecting the natural or industrial environment. The industrial waste water is continuously sensed from a pH sensor. If the pH level is not maintained within the standard value, this information will be sent directly to the pollution control board through the IoT module. Another important step is that the pH level present in the industrial waste during the treatment can be continuously monitored through the internet by using a web page (cloud). Thus this system will monitor and control waste water pollution efficiently and the data can be transferred through cloud communication. A Graphical User Interface (GUI) Cayenne is used for monitoring and IoT is used for real-time interaction as well as data transfer.

abstract: This paper asks whether the Italian stock market prices the acts of capital-goods incentive policy (Transizione 4.0, Transizione 5.0, Nuova Transizione 5.0) when they are issued, and whether a large language model (LLM) reading those acts can extract a signal that the market incorporates with a lag. A corpus of 37 legislative and administrative acts between April 2019 and June 2026 is coded manually and, independently and blind, by an LLM; concordance is near-complete on category and date, substantial on intensity and moderate on expected sign. A market-model event study on 30 directional events and a two-tier basket of eight Euronext Milan stocks (domestic users of incentivised assets and suppliers of eligible capital goods) finds no abnormal return after the event under any coding: signed CAAR of +0.09% on [+1, +5] and +0.39% on [0, +5] under the manual coding, both indistinguishable from zero; a publication-day estimate of +0.29% that does not survive multiple-testing correction, the Corrado rank test, the Kolari-Pynnönen cross-correlation adjustment, the clustering of overlapping acts or the LLM coding. The result holds at the political-announcement date, is robust to estimation windows, basket composition and a survivorship control, and has a minimum detectable effect of about 1.5%. A post hoc hypothesis that the direction of acts follows the sector cycle is rejected on machine-tool orders and on official Eurostat data: the direction of an act is explained by its administrative nature (industrial policy versus spending control). The contribution is a documented negative result on a source of unstructured open data not covered by the financial text-mining literature.
title: Do Capital-Goods Incentive Announcements Move Italian Industrial Stocks? An Event Study with LLM-Coded Regulatory Acts, 2019–2026

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) agents are increasingly deployed for voltage control in power distribution networks. However, their opaque decision-making creates a significant trust barrier, limiting their adoption in safety-sensitive operational settings. This paper presents XRL-LLM, a novel framework that generates natural language explanations for RL control decisions by combining game-theoretic feature attribution (KernelSHAP) with large language model (LLM) reasoning grounded in power systems domain knowledge.We deployed a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent on an IEEE 33-bus network to coordinate capacitor banks, tap changers, and shunt regulators, successfully reducing voltage violations by 90.5% across diverse loading conditions. To make these decisions interpretable, KernelSHAP identifies the most influential state features. These features are then processed by a domain-context-engineered LLM prompt that explicitly encodes network topology, device specifications, and ANSI C84.1 voltage limits.Evaluated via G-Eval across 30 scenarios, XRL-LLM achieves an explanation quality score of 4.13/5. This represents a 33.7% improvement over template-based generation and a 67.9% improvement over raw SHAP outputs, delivering statistically significant gains in accuracy, actionability, and completeness (p&lt; 0.001, Cohen’s d values up to 4.07). Additionally, a physics-grounded counterfactual verification procedure which perturbs the underlying power flow model, confirms a causal faithfulness of 0.81 under critical loading.
title: XRL-LLM: Explainable Reinforcement Learning Framework for Voltage Control

abstract: This paper presents an empirical analysis of a constraint-based dialogue control architecture applied to large language models (LLMs), with additional focus on multi-agent coordination dynamics. Through structured dialogue experiments conducted within AkaneCore-based multi-persona coexistence chat systems, we examine how explicit behavioral constraints influence responses under conditions of misinformation, error, uncertainty, and infeasible requests, and how multi-agent interaction affects response stability. The experimental environment consists of two AkaneCore implementations: Izakaya Phase (Gemini Gems platform, 11 personas) and Maruti Agent Council (ChatGPT GPTs platform, 3 agents). Both systems operate under the Unified Emotional Responsibility Architecture (U.E.R.A.), which defines shared behavioral principles including responsibility triggers, persona-specific responsibility intensity, and dialogue continuity requirements. Results indicate that constraint-based control induces systematic behavioral shifts toward verification-oriented and responsibility-aware responses, while multi-agent coordination introduces additional interaction dynamics including role differentiation and emergent response ordering. Crucially, the analysis reveals that initial constraint bypass can occur in personas with low responsibility trigger thresholds, with correction emerging only after external challenge. Dialogue logs collected from author-conducted sessions are presented in Appendix C as primary evidence.
title: Empirical Analysis of Constraint-Based Dialogue Control and Multi-Agent Coordination in LLM Systems

abstract: During nuclear station refurbishment, transportation of tools, equipment, and irradiated reactor components is achieved using remote guided vehicles (RGV’s) in order to keep worker radiation doses as low as reasonably achievable. A removable guardrail system capable of withstanding RGV impact was developed to eliminate the risk of accidents taking place in the reactor vault. The guardrails are mounted to platform edges using two bolts and two shear pins. In anticipation of frequent removal of reinstallation of guardrails by workers, this study proposes that guardrails be installed without bolting, relying solely on the guardrails’ shear pins to provide the required restraint. A parametric impact simulation was carried out in order to evaluate the perform of the guardrails when installed without bolting. The analysis work was carried out using LS-DYNA, an advanced simulation software package capable of simulating real world problems using explicit time integration.
title: Guardrail impact simulation for remote guided vehicles (RGV's) used in nuclear generating stations

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in educational platforms through instructable behavioral guardrails encoded as system prompts (e.g., "do not solve homework problems for students''). However, safety alignment in modern LLMs is predominantly English-centric, leaving their behavior in other languages underexplored. We present a two-phase study using EduRobust, a reproducible benchmarking framework for multilingual system prompt robustness. In Phase 1 we measure the vulnerability gap: 5 educational behavioral restrictions are tested across 24 languages, 3 open-source LLMs, and 50 repeated trials per configuration (18,000 cells). In Phase 2 we test three candidate defenses: (A) strategy-aware prompt hardening, (B) multilingual system prompts, and (C) composite English-only anchoring. The inverted resource-tier gradient persists under all three defenses, and multilingual model capability proves to be a double-edged sword --- amplifying both attack susceptibility and defense responsiveness. We release the full framework; including attack templates, translation cache, defense variants, evaluation harness, and analysis scripts; to support reproducible multilingual safety research in the educational AI community.
title: EduRobust: Multilingual Robustness of System Prompt Restrictions in Educational LLM Deployments

abstract: Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) have revolutionized education by offering personalized learning experiences. However, as goal-oriented learning, which emphasizes efficiently achieving specific objectives, becomes increasingly important in professional contexts, existing ITSs often struggle to deliver this type of targeted learning experience. In this paper, we propose GenMentor, an LLM-powered multi-agent framework designed to deliver goal-oriented, personalized learning within ITS. GenMentor begins by accurately mapping learners' goals to required skills using a fine-tuned LLM trained on a custom goal-to-skill dataset. After identifying the skill gap, it schedules an efficient learning path using an evolving optimization approach, driven by a comprehensive and dynamic profile of learners' multifaceted status. Additionally, GenMentor tailors learning content with an exploration-drafting-integration mechanism to align with individual learner needs. Extensive automated and human evaluations demonstrate GenMentor's effectiveness in learning guidance and content quality. Furthermore, we have deployed it in practice and also implemented it as an application. Practical human study with professional learners further highlights its effectiveness in goal alignment and resource targeting, leading to enhanced personalization. Supplementary resources are available at https://github.com/GeminiLight/gen-mentor.
title: LLM-powered Multi-agent Framework for Goal-oriented Learning in Intelligent Tutoring System

abstract: Tool-augmented language model agents create a queueing-control problem under firm deadlines: enabling a tool-rich inference pipeline can improve expected utility, but it also increases service time, variability, and deadlinemiss risk. We study this setting as a non-preemptive single-server queue with abandonment at deadlines and two execution modes: a tool-rich slow mode with higher expected utility and a tool-restricted fast mode with shorter service times.We propose Firm-Deadline Tool Control (FTC), an arrival-epoch queueingcontrol policy that selects between a tool-rich slow mode and a tool-restricted fast mode based on predicted deadline feasibility. Beyond the procedural rule, we show that FTC has an exact monotone threshold structure in estimated backlog, TTL, and the time-margin parameter ε. A single multiplicative margin parameter, ε, controls the operating point and traces a utility–miss-rate frontier. We further prove that the threshold structure of FTC extends beyond the binary fast/slow setting to a finite ordered multimode menu, showing that the richest feasible mode is selected by an exact tier-threshold rule in estimated backlog and TTL.Using trace-driven discrete-event simulation calibrated with paired counterfactual fast/slow latency traces collected from three local tool-augmented LLM backends (Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, and Mistral 7B Instruct), we compare FTC against fixed-mode, heuristic, bang-bang, and drift-style baselines. Across multiple TTL regimes, FTC consistently improves the utility–miss-rate balance over coarse queue-threshold and heuristic comparators in tight settings, while remaining tunable through the time-margin parameter ε as deadlines become more permissive. The policy layer is not tied to one specific foundation model: it depends on queue state, deadlines, and calibrated mode-wise latency summaries, so other tool-augmented LLM stacks can be incorporated by replacing the empirical trace source.
title: Tool-Augmented LLM Serving Under Firm Deadlines: A Queueing-Control Approach

abstract: Swarm robotic systems consist of a large number of distributed autonomous robots that coordinate their actions to accomplish diverse tasks beyond the capabilities of a single robot. These systems have recently been considered for deployment in disaster scenarios, where communication is often unstable, making it necessary to achieve adaptive cooperative behavior without relying on explicit communication between robots. In the context of multi-robot systems—including swarm robotic systems—some studies have explored approaches utilizing large language models (LLMs) or other learning-based methods, but few have proposed systems that enable communication-free coordination. In this paper, we propose a system incorporating a novel method that combines high-level decision-making via LLM-based policy selection—guided by questionnaire-style prompts—with low-level control using multiple MARL-trained policies. We consider a complex task scenario in which robots search for a target object and transport it to a designated destination. To evaluate the method, we define implicit consensus as a condition in which a robot selects the same policy as its nearby robots without any explicit communication. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through simulated task execution, with particular emphasis on implicit consensus as a key evaluation metric.
title: Communication-Free Adaptive Swarm Robotic System: LLM-Based Decision Making and MARL-Based Multi-Policy Control

abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop an integrated sensing–perception–control system for automated highway guardrail installation, addressing the depth perception failure of RGB-D cameras over hollow structural regions in field working conditions. Design/methodology/approach An edge-exterior multilayer depth sampling strategy with 72 points on three concentric rings is proposed to obtain reliable surface depth from the solid body surrounding the hollow aperture under oblique viewing and partial occlusion. A lightweight segmentation model, YOLOv11n-PMS-seg, adopts a feature optimization–attention enhancement–shape constraint design, supported by ellipse fitting, Kalman filtering, track-ID recovery and adaptive CAN transmission. A one-time teaching step records the relative pose between the gripper and hole; the manipulator servos to this reference, eliminating explicit hand-eye calibration and making grasping invariant to forklift position and guardrail height. Findings The depth acquisition success rate reaches 99.4%. Under a single calibration at 1,250 mm, localization error is 17.8 ± 4.2 mm at 30 fps. Across 200 outdoor winter trials (−5 to 5 °C), 194 were successful; the six failures manifested as system-level freezes rather than as erroneous perception output. For low-illumination indoor scenes, a 6 W LED supplementary light maintains depth quality. YOLOv11n-PMS-seg cuts parameters by 7.8% and GFLOPs by 10.7% while improving mAP@0.5:0.95 by 3.3 percentage points. Research limitations/implications The system is currently validated at a fixed vertical distance of 1,250 mm for single-target scenarios. Failure attribution relied on field observation, as automated telemetry logging was not implemented. Future work should address variable operating distances, multi-target grasping and onboard failure diagnosis to broaden deployment applicability. Practical implications The proposed system enables automated robotic grasping of hollow guardrail components with a 97.0% success rate under real outdoor conditions, directly reducing manual labor and safety risks in highway construction. Its lightweight architecture (17% GPU utilization) allows integration into existing industrial vehicle platforms without significant hardware upgrades, offering a cost-effective solution for infrastructure automation. Social implications Automating highway guardrail installation reduces worker exposure to traffic hazards and physically demanding labor in road construction environments. Validated outdoor winter deployment demonstrates the feasibility of year-round infrastructure maintenance, contributing to safer roads and more efficient use of construction resources in civil engineering applications. Originality/value This work presents an integrated grasping pipeline for hollow guardrail components that combines a geometry-based depth sampling strategy with a teaching-based relative-pose scheme, without relying on additional learning-based depth completion networks. Validation covers winter outdoor daytime conditions at a single calibration distance; rainfall, direct sunlight and other guardrail specifications remain future work.
title: Robotic grasping of hollow guardrail components for outdoor installation: a geometry-based RGB-D depth sampling approach for 3D localization

abstract: Industrial control systems are often used to assist and manage an industrial operation. These systems’ weaknesses in the various hierarchical structures of the system components and communication backbones make them vulnerable to cyberattacks that jeopardize their security. In this paper, the security of these systems is studied by employing a reinforcement learning extended attack graph to efficiently reveal the subsystems’ flaws. Specifically, an attack graph that mimics the environment is constructed for the system using the state–action–reward–state–action technique, in which the agent is regarded as the attacker. Attackers may cause the greatest amount of system damage with the fewest possible actions if they have the highest cumulative reward. The worst-case assault scheme with a total reward of 42.9 was successfully shown in the results, and the most badly affected subsystems were recognized.
title: Security Assessment of Industrial Control System Applying Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In control engineering, the control of an unstable system is very concerning. An example of an unstable system that uses control principles is a ball and beam balancer system. This system consists of a long beam attached to a motor at its midpoint. A steel ball moves on the top of the beam with an acceleration proportional to the beam angle. If the system is uncontrolled well, the steel ball may fall from the beam. This paper presents an approach to modeling and controlling the ball position for the ball and beam balancer system. Starting with a mathematical equation for the nonlinear system, the model of the system is produced. Then, it demonstrates the design of the PID cascade controller system to stabilize the system and regulate the ball to its reference position. The performance of the system was evaluated and tested for set-point tracking signal and disturbance rejection test. The simulation studies were done using Matlab Simulink and the results indicated that the proposed approach yields robust closed-loop performance.
title: PID Cascade Controller Design for an Unstable System

abstract: A metaverse is a virtual convergence environment that promotes inclusiveness and diversity by maintaining social relationships among users through avatars and engaging them in various cultural activities. Because everyday activities can be maintained the same in a metaverse environment, the transmission, exchange, and sharing of useful and accurate information among members in the metaverse environment has become important. Additionally, the desire and requirements of members to obtain the desired information through conversations with avatars in a metaverse are increasing; the number of these cases is also increasing. Accordingly, in this study, we redesigned and implemented the structure of the metaverse platform at Korea Polytechnics such that generative AI based on an LLM could be utilized on the metaverse platform. By presenting experimental examples according to the implementation, we confirmed that an AI-based service could be provided that configured the LLM and generated answers in the metaverse. In future research, we plan to apply various generative AI models to the metaverse platform, present a customized model through a comparative analysis, and continue research on implementing our LLM model.
title: Implementation of Generative AI Using Metaverse-Based LLM

abstract: Current evaluation of large language models (LLMs) predominantly relies on short-horizon, reset-based interactions designed to assess task performance under controlled conditions. While effective for measuring capability, such regimes structurally limit observation of behaviors that emerge only through sustained interaction—and leave behavioral reliability over extended interaction largely uncharacterized.This paper introduces a qualitative, non-scalable observational method for examining LLM behavior under extended, non-reset conversational conditions, and documents failure modes observed when epistemic pressure weakened or interactional dynamics accumulated unchecked. The observed phenomena range from mild conversational tendencies to substantive failures that produced incorrect outputs, masked errors, or misleading confidence. Two failure modes – Narrative Arc Confabulation and Instance Identity Confusion – are not explicitly named or taxonomized in the literature reviewed as of early 2026 and may represent under-documented phenomena.The paper further examines why awareness of these failure modes does not suffice to prevent them, arguing that long-horizon stability depends on practiced, situational human judgment that resists procedural transfer. The contribution is descriptive and clarificatory: defining an observational space that prevailing evaluation practices structurally exclude, documenting phenomena that emerge within that space, and explaining why reliability under extended interaction is conditional, costly, and human-dependent.
title: Long-Horizon Reliability in Human–LLM Interaction: Observations, Failure Modes, and Limits of Procedural Control

abstract: Abstract Building and refining cryo-EM atomic models often requires long, project-specific workflows that combine map inspection, prior structural knowledge, restraints, refinement, validation and expert review. Existing programs perform many individual operations, but coordinating them across iterative model-building sessions remains manual and difficult to audit. We present StructAgent, a user-guided multi-agent resource for cryo-EM model building and refinement. StructAgent couples a domain agent for literature-grounded structural reasoning with an execution agent that runs local software, tracks state, recovers from failures and records provenance. Expert approval gates control major model-changing actions. In three case studies, StructAgent refitted a 64-chain proteasome from an earlier template, audited 530 ribosomal metal-ion sites and guided a chemically ambiguous ligand fit in a folate-metabolism enzyme from ongoing work. These demonstrations show that agentic orchestration can convert modeling intent into auditable, reviewable software workflows while preserving expert control and final scientific judgment.
title: StructAgent: Orchestrating Cryo-EM Model Building and Refinement with a Multi-Agent LLM System

abstract: Analogical reasoning-the science of similarity and comparison-is indispensable in domains where evidence is sparse, delayed, or incomplete. Classical Dempster-Shafer Theory (DST) provides a principled foundation for reasoning under uncertainty, but it becomes unstable when evidence is weak or or when systems exhibit time-delayed reaction. This work arises from the need to make reliable engineering decisions when evidence is sparse, uncertain, and must be interpreted through causation-aware analogical reasoning. The objective of this paper is to develop a theory of Relational Analogical Knowledge Assessment that integrates causal-relational structure, coarse-grained belief representation, and temporal evidence evolution, and to construct a guardrail framework that stabilizes belief fusion under sparse or uncertain evidence using expert-defined thresholds and dependability classes that map analogical proximity into operational fusion strategies. The method further constructs a framework by modeling a causal relational skeleton, defining an operator that evaluates analogical proximity and restricts evidence transfer to causally valid pathways, and representing uncertainty through coarse-grained belief states that stabilize reasoning under sparse or noisy data. It incorporates a belief-evolution mechanism to handle temporally unfolding evidence and delayed system reactions, and embeds a guardrail framework that detects and mitigates unstable or inappropriate belief updates. The approach further incorporates expert-defined thresholds and dependability classes to translate analogical distance into context-appropriate fusion strategies, yielding a causation-aware, guardrail-stabilized extension of DST for reliable analogical reasoning in engineering settings. The application of this approach are highly relevant to process-engineering domains involving geological, chemical, or biological systems, e.g., oil and gas operations, pipeline integrity management, grain preservation, drug discovery or complex medical treatments. This research aligns with the ongoing development of a theoretical foundation for the patented CausX AI framework that is being adopted in the oil and gas industry, laying the groundwork for a progressively more robust and unified paradigm applicable to other high stake engineering domains.
title: A Relational Analogical Knowledge Assessment Theory Under Uncertainty with a Guardrail Based Framework

abstract: Abstract Agent-oriented large language model applications require runtime controls that connect detection, risk representation, proportionate response, human oversight, and reviewable evidence. This article reports an artefact-based software case study of AgentGuard AI v2.4.0, a research prototype that operationalises the Secure Runtime Monitoring Protocol (SRMP), Adaptive Agent Risk Scoring (AARS), and Risk-Adaptive Scheduling and State Control (RASS). Evidence was triangulated from author-supplied design records, the public deployment inspected on 27 August 2026, and a downloaded archive from one 25-event synthetic smoke test. The prototype combines a 23-rule monitoring library, six risk dimensions, four control states, role-based access, privacy options, audit chaining, replay, statistical views, standards traceability, and report export in a Python 3.11 Streamlit application. The inspected deployment exposed 23 functional pages plus an overview, extending the documented 17-page baseline. The synthetic run completed and produced raw events, alerts, risk scores, actions, configuration, metrics, and checksums. It also exposed material reproducibility defects: the interface and archive disagreed on the active AARS version; seed and source-commit fields were absent; and the exported high-risk action records did not match the exported policy mapping. These observations show that AgentGuard AI is an inspectable, governance-aware research instrument, but do not establish detection effectiveness, production enforcement, or operational reliability. The contribution is a bounded reference pattern for connecting runtime risk analytics with human review and evidence, together with an explicit account of the validation work still required.
title: Runtime Risk Detection and Control for AI Agents and LLM Applications

abstract: Abstract The quality and integrity of scientific publications in clinical machine-learning is of paramount importance. Low-quality publications can offer excessively optimistic estimates of model performance, leading to unrealistic expectations when translating models to clinical scenarios. In radiomics this is no less the case: recent studies have highlighted the stark publication bias in radiomics research, and multiple investigations showed how radiomics-based research can be affected by several methodological confounders. To address this systematically, the Radiomics Quality Score (RQS) and the METhodological RadiomICs Score (METRICS) were designed. Both provide a standardised quantity determining the methodological quality of radiomics scientific manuscripts, thus validating their clinical translation. METRICS, out of the two, has been shown to be more reproducible and accurate. In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have been used in many science-related tasks. Here, we ask the following question: how are LLM-based METRICS assessments correlated with those performed by radiologists? Using two recent reproducibility studies, we provide evidence that LLM-based radiomics assessments can be a useful assistant in determining the scientific quality of radiomics-based publications. Particularly, we show that inter-rater agreements between LLMs and human raters are similar to those reported between human raters. Additionally, we also show that the correlation and error between METRICS scores obtained by human raters and LLMs is similar to those obtained between human raters. These results constitute an important proof of concept — LLMs can be used to assist human raters in deriving standardised scores. Keypoints Question How well do LLM-based METRICS assessments correlate with those performed by radiologists in determining the scientific quality of radiomics-based publications, addressing the need for efficient quality control? Findings LLM-based radiomics assessments demonstrate inter-rater agreements with human raters similar to those between human raters, suggesting their utility in assisting with standardized scoring. Clinical Relevance Statement LLMs can assist in the standardized assessment of radiomics research quality, potentially improving the reliability and clinical translatability of radiomics-based tools by ensuring studies meet rigorous methodological standards, ultimately benefiting patient care through more robust clinical applications.
title: Auto-METRICS: LLM-assisted scientific quality control for radiomics research

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong performance across biomedical and clinical tasks, yet their deployment in healthcare remains limited by hallucination. Prior research has often treated hallucination as an isolated model failure to be addressed through improved training, prompting, or retrieval. However, emerging theoretical and empirical evidence suggests that hallucination is instead a structural property of probabilistic language generation rather than a fully removable bug. This distinction is particularly critical in medicine and healthcare, where near-correct answers, fabricated evidence, and unsafe recommendations can introduce real patient risk and legal liability. In this paper, we present a system-level survey of hallucination in medical LLMs. Rather than exhaustively cataloging every prior work, our goal is to highlight the dominant research directions and analyze the problem from a systems perspective. We synthesize literature spanning definitions, taxonomies, benchmarks, detection methods, and mitigation strategies, and examine how these components interact within real clinical workflows. Our analysis shows that despite diverse models and technical advances, improvements to individual components rarely translate into reliable end-to-end systems. Based on this synthesis, we argue that hallucination in healthcare should be treated as a system-level risk management problem rather than a model-level defect. We outline key open challenges and emphasize the need to understand not only how to reduce hallucinations, but why they occur and how their impact propagates through clinical decision pipelines. Ultimately, progress toward trustworthy medical AI will depend on designing systems that anticipate, monitor, and safely manage hallucinations rather than assuming they can be fully eliminated.
title: Rethinking Medical LLM Hallucinations: A System-Level Survey

abstract: The growing demands of Industry 4.0 require advanced robotic systems, characterized by efficient, precise, and robust motion planning and control. The benefits offered by traditional robotic motion planning and control optimization methods often include high cost of design, limited ability to generalize due to tuning parameters manually, and poor interpretability due to complex mathematical models. In this paper, we propose a dual-modal prompt engineering approach, known as Ours, that combines instantiation for reasoning with recent advancements in (neural) large language models alongside structured numerical data from robotic systems. The approach interprets both natural Language task descriptions and quantitative parameters of the robot in order to plan optimal motions and control strategies. A process of Closed-Loop Optimization iteratively improves results based upon feedback from a simulated environment. Results from evaluating on an industrial robotic arm show that Our can achieve faster optimization and better control precision, stability, and robustness under changing conditions than traditional design baselines and in single modal comparison. We highlight the new possibilities of using (neural) large language models as intelligent actors.
title: A Dual-Modal Prompt Framework for LLM-Assisted Robotic Motion Planning and Control Optimization

abstract: Abstract The parent of an adolescent patient noticed an upcoming appointment in the patient's portal account that should have remained confidential to the parent. As it turned out, this parent was directly accessing their child's adolescent patient portal account instead of using a proxy account. After investigation of this case, it was found that the adolescent account had been activated with the parent's demographic (i.e., phone/email) information. This case illustrates the challenges of using adult-centric electronic health record (EHR) systems and how our institution addressed the problem of incorrect portal account activations. Confidentiality is fundamental to providing healthcare to adolescents. To comply with the 21st Century Cures Act's information blocking rules, confidential information must be released to adolescent patients when appropriate while also remaining confidential from their guardians. While complying with this national standard, systems of care must also account for interstate variability in which services allow for confidential adolescent consent. Unfortunately, there are high rates of guardian access to adolescent portal accounts which may lead to unintended disclosure of confidential information. Therefore, measures must be taken to minimize the risk of inadvertent confidentiality breaches via adolescent patient portals. Our institution implemented a guardrail system that checks the adolescent patient's contact information against the contact information of their parent/guardian/guarantor. This guardrail reduced the rate of account activation errors after implementation. However, the guardrail can be bypassed when demographic fields are missing. Thus, ongoing efforts to create pediatric-appropriate demographic fields, clearly distinguishing patient from proxy, in the EHR and workflows for registration of proxy accounts in the patient portal are needed.
title: Creating a Guardrail System to Ensure Appropriate Activation of Adolescent Portal Accounts

abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for C++ code generation, yet their ability to satisfy Motor Industry Software Reliability Association (MISRA) C++:2023 guidelines at scale remains unclear. This study conducts a controlled before–after, repeated-measures study on 26 C++ tasks, evaluating four models with 20 runs per condition. Compiled outputs are checked with a complete MISRA C++:2023 ruleset. Verbose rule texts are distilled into compact, actionable Top-k instruction packs (k=3,5,10) targeting each model’s most frequent violations. Primary outcomes are violations per thousand lines of code (KLOC), compile rate, and pass rate. At baseline, models cluster at 23–29 violations/KLOC, dominated by an advisory rule discouraging standard integer type names. Adding Top-k instructions reduces violations by 44–83% across models (paired permutation tests, all p < 0.01); GPT-5 and o3 reach 3.9–4.5 violations/KLOC. Functional impacts are small overall; two conditions show significant pass-rate declines (GPT-4.1/Top-3, o3/Top-10). Improvements spill over to non-targeted rules. Compact, model-aware MISRA prompts therefore offer a practical path to safer C++ generation with limited functional cost when scoped appropriately. However, full verification still requires dedicated compliance tooling to detect residual issues, quantify results for certification, and produce auditable evidence for regulators. Practitioners should adopt a step-up strategy, start with Top-3 or Top-5 rules, monitor compile and pass rates, and expand only when stable. Study artifacts are released to enable replication and reuse.
title: Reducing MISRA violations in LLM-generated code by 83%: An empirical study with static analysis verification
Towards Automated Reasoning Chains for Verification of LLM-Generated Scientific Code

abstract: The rapid adoption of large language model (LLM) based code generation tools in commercial software development has created a governance gap between code production speed and code quality assurance. This paper examines how human-in-the-loop (HITL) governance structures can address that gap by embedding engineering accountability, automated verification gates, and structured review protocols into AI-augmented development workflows. Drawing on a systematic review of 20 peer-reviewed and industry-authoritative sources, the study maps the principal failure modes of LLM-generated code, evaluates existing oversight frameworks, and proposes an original five-phase Engineering Control and Verification Model (ECVM) that assigns explicit responsibility to both automated toolchains and human engineers at each lifecycle stage. Empirical evidence shows that developers complete repetitive coding tasks up to 55 % faster with AI assistance, yet acceptance of AI suggestions without review correlates with measurable increases in security defects and logical errors. The proposed model offers software engineering teams a structured path to realizing productivity gains while preserving code integrity. The findings are relevant to software engineering practitioners, technical leads, and organizations designing AI-augmented development processes.
title: Human-in-the-Loop Governance for LLM-Generated Code: An Engineering Control, Accountability, and Verification Model in AI-Augmented Software Development
venue: EJSMT

abstract: Background: LLM-generated synthetic code is now a standard ingredient in code-LM training, but its quality is rarely audited before entering the fine-tune loop. The de facto n-gram contamination check over-flags universal boilerplate and under-flags problem-level paraphrase, and the literature lacks a structured measurement scaffold to take its place.Methods: We propose an audit taxonomy with operational framework for LLM-generated synthetic code, mapped to ISO/IEC 25010 software-quality characteristics. The taxonomy organises nine dimensions into three operational bands (contamination, structural-and-semantic, execution), embeds a rule-based two-axis contamination diagnostic with four operationally distinct cells, and is exposed through a deterministic open-source Python implementation. We apply the audit taxonomy to five public synthetic-code datasets and validate it downstream by LoRA-fine-tuning code-LMs across three Qwen-Coder sizes, StarCoder2-3B, and DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B on MBPP-500 and HumanEval.Results: Four strong-signal axes discriminate the datasets at medium-to-large multi-seed effect sizes (Friedman p <= 0.0012 on every strong axis). A uniform-weight five-axis composite rank-orders the five datasets against MBPP-500 pass@1 within the Qwen-Coder family (Spearman rho >= +0.70); cross-family transfer is partial on StarCoder2-3B (rho = +0.60) and does not hold on DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B (rho = -0.20). HumanEval inverts the ordering, showing benchmark-contingent predictivity.Conclusions: The audit taxonomy discriminates synthetic-code datasets consistently and supplies a reusable knowledge artefact for synthetic-data quality assurance. Downstream predictivity is family- and benchmark-contingent; we report it as bounded validation evidence rather than a general predictivity claim.
title: Auditing Synthetic Code: A Multi-Dimensional Taxonomy and Evaluation Framework for LLM-Generated Code Training Data

abstract: Context: The growing adoption of large language models (LLMs) in software development creates a need for reliable code provenance verification to support review and accountability. However, source code watermarking must accommodate strict functional constraints and withstand subsequent code modifications.Objective: This study investigates whether post-generation syntactic watermarking can reliably identify watermarked LLM-generated code while limiting correctness degradation and remaining detectable after routine edits and deliberate removal attempts.Method: We propose CREST (Code Robust Embedding via Syntactic Transformations), a model-agnostic framework for Python that iteratively applies 49 concrete syntax tree transformations without accessing model internals. A supervised probabilistic detector learns watermark evidence from clean and manipulated programs. We evaluate discriminability, functional correctness, and resilience using more than 26,000 artifacts derived from HumanEval+, MBPP, and APPS, including GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-Coder solutions, with task-level training and test splits.Results: At the calibrated operating point, CREST achieves a 100\% true positive rate and a 1.23% false positive rate on the clean test set. Watermark embedding reduces pass@1 by a weighted average of 0.90 percentage points. Detection retains a 98.24% true positive rate after a four-stage pipeline combining identifier renaming, structural refactoring, standardization, and noise injection, and 94.70--98.40% under attack configurations unseen during training.Conclusions: The results support combining post-generation syntactic watermarking with robustness-aware probabilistic detection for code provenance verification. CREST maintains high detection rates under the evaluated modifications with limited functional degradation, motivating further validation in repository-scale development workflows.
title: Detecting LLM-Generated Source Code via Robust Watermarking
Investigating Code Similarity Patterns in LLM-Generated and Human-Written Programming Solutions
